newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE - South Africa debates issue of foreign workers.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - South Africa debates issue of foreign workers.

text.p: South Africans are losing patience with migrants who flock to the country to take scarce jobs, but an expert study of the problem says an influx of foreigners is not all bad.
The country's powerful unions, seeing business rub its hands at the prospect of even cheaper labour, are wary about any dramatic change in policy, as is the government.

Unveiling three years of research into immigration, a prominent South African think-tank said in a new report that growing regional trade and opening markets meant a blanket restriction on immigration was neither possible nor desirable.

"South Africa will not become a successful world competitor as a closed, nationalistic, narrow society," the Centre for Development and Enterprise said in the report, which proposes that immigrants be allowed in to prove their worth.
"(The country) is perennially short of skilled and entrepreneurial people. Economic growth requires as many skills as we can grow, hire and import."
Under pressure at home to crack down on illegal immigration, yet faced with inadequate border controls and the high costs of deportation, Pretoria has begun a review of the current laws.
"We've moved into a new government with new ideas. In this transformation process, immigration policy would also have to transform," Home Affairs spokesman Hennie Meyer told Reuters.
"But it's a long process," he cautioned. The deadline for public comment on the government's legislative review expires on June 30.

South Africa was fostered by immigrants -- ranging from the ancestors of many blacks who migrated from central Africa to scores of Dutch, German, French and British settlers -- but the immigration issue has become a political hot potato for President Nelson Mandela's post-apartheid democracy.
IMMIGRANTS TAKE BLAME FOR ALL WOES
Estimates show the country has more than two million illegal immigrants, mostly from neighbouring Mozambique and Zimbabwe -- about 15 percent of the national workforce.
A recent study on unemployment found that 79 percent of South Africans saw them as the main cause.
Many also blame rampant crime on "illegals", particularly West Africans, who are rebuffed as drug dealers and conmen.

Mooting the unconditional acceptance of skilled immigrants, the Centre for Development and Enterprise said that, as a developing country, South Africa should broaden this definition to include entrepreneurs in the formal and informal sector.

Unskilled workers from the 12-nation Southern African Development Community (SADC) should be allowed into the country for a six-month trial and permitted to remain if they could prove that they had found jobs and a fixed home address, the Centre said.

"No doubt some will criticise...this as being altogether too lenient. But if those critics object to the presence in this country of people who bring skills with them, who are able to support themselves, who pay their taxes and abide by our laws, then they do so simply because they are foreigners.
"We do not believe such objections are valid," said the Centre, whose board includes respected business leaders and political economists.

"It is important to see migration as a valuable additional source of human capital, which creates opportunities for more rapid growth, rather than as a source of competition for a fixed number of jobs."
BUSINESS HUNGERS, LABOUR TIPTOES

Economist Dave Mohr, promoting the free movement of capital, goods and labour, said that while South Africa had been unsuccessful in keeping out unskilled labour, it had been able to control the legal influx of skilled people.
"What we need are fewer restrictions and consistency," said Mohr, from South Africa's biggest investment group, Old Mutual.
"There should be a general freeing up of all the various factors of production. In trying to restrict them, you usually end up creating more obstacles."

Mohr acknowledged that a wholesale deregulation of immigration would have serious consequences for the labour market and could force a reversal of the increasingly rigid labour policy the government favoured, but said he believed this was necessary.
"It will probably force certain labour market reforms, but if you look at our job market, it's not geared to job creation."
South Africa's giant Cosatu trade union federation has consistently spoken out against xenophobia, but a total relaxation of regulations would materially affect its two million members.
Cosatu has only recently won labour-friendly legislation, owing to its alliance with Mandela's ruling party.

Spokeswoman Noweto Mpati said the federation favoured the formation of a regional regulatory forum which could determine minimum working conditions in SADC states, and help promote a southern African investment drive.

"We are not saying there should be minimum salaries," she said. "But there should be labour standards for the region, thereby addressing the question of immigrant workers being victimised by employers."
